701: Learning. The one dial you already own.
702: Every time you practise something, your brain physically rewires itself. Connections you use get stronger. Connections you ignore fade.
703: London taxi drivers have to memorise around twenty-five thousand streets. In brain scans, the back part of their hippocampus, a region involved in navigation, was larger than in other people.
704: And you don't need a taxi licence. In one study, people who practised juggling for three months showed measurable changes in their brain scans. When they stopped, the changes partly faded again.
705: So, dial at maximum. Every lesson sticks the first time. A new song, a new language, a new trick on the board.
706: In reality, no dial goes that high. But two tricks come surprisingly close. First: spread your practice over several days, instead of cramming it into one night.
707: Second: sleep. In rats, scientists watched the brain cells that fired while running a maze fire again during sleep, in the same order. The brain was replaying the day.
708: Verdict: learning is the dial that really turns. Slowly, but for real.
709: Okay. Time for the big fantasy questions. With a brain at one hundred percent, could you travel through time?
710: Sadly, no. Time travel is a physics problem, not a brain problem. But your brain can bend how time feels.
711: In one experiment, volunteers dropped backwards from a tower, about thirty metres high, into a safety net. Afterwards, they guessed that their own fall had lasted about a third longer than other people's falls.
712: They weren't seeing in slow motion. Their brains were saving more memories, so the moment felt longer looking back.
713: Next question. Could you read minds? No telepathy, sorry. But your brain reads faces fast. In one study, a tenth of a second was enough for people to form a first impression of a stranger.
714: And could you see colours nobody else can? Quick side note first. Your eye has three types of colour cells, roughly for red, green and blue. Every colour you see is a mix of those three.
715: That's also why a rainbow has no real stripes. It's one smooth blend. Isaac Newton simply chose seven colours, partly to match the seven notes of a musical scale.
716: Now the strange part. A few people may carry a fourth type of colour cell. In one study, one woman could tell apart colours that looked identical to everyone else in the test.
717: So no time machine. No mind reading. But a brain that stretches time, reads faces in a blink, and sometimes sees extra colours? Honestly, not bad.
718: Which leaves one last question. Is there a real version of one hundred percent?
